title: Adaptive Switching Between Parallel-World Self-Correction and Mutual Correction for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate incorrect, incomplete, or internally inconsistent responses. Self-correction allows a model to inspect and revise its own outputs, whereas mutual correction enables multiple model instances or heterogeneous models to identify and address one another's errors. However, relying exclusively on either mechanism may limit the diversity of corrective perspectives, increase computational costs, or reinforce existing mistakes. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Self-Correction and Mutual Correction (APSMC), a unified framework in which multiple LLMs dynamically switch between independent self-correction and collaborative mutual correction according to the observed characteristics of their outputs and the estimated benefits of further interaction. The framework introduces parallel worlds, defined as independently maintained corrective trajectories generated by the same underlying model under different correction objectives, prompts, reasoning constraints, or contextual perspectives. Each trajectory performs self-correction before selectively exchanging information with other trajectories. An adaptive controller determines whether the system should continue independent correction, initiate pairwise mutual correction, activate group-level correction, or terminate the process. The framework also supports heterogeneous LLMs that participate in correction without belonging to the same parallel-world group. Unlike fixed self-correction and permanently collaborative architectures, APSMC treats the choice between independent and collaborative correction as a dynamic decision-making problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents a correction-selection algorithm, defines evaluation metrics, and proposes an experimental protocol for assessing accuracy, correction reliability, diversity, computational efficiency, and resistance to collective errors. The framework is a research proposal; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing methods require systematic empirical validation.

Unlike fixed self-correction and permanently collaborative architectures, APSMC treats the choice between independent and collaborative correction as a dynamic decision-making problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents a correction-selection algorithm, defines evaluation metrics, and proposes an experimental protocol for assessing accuracy, correction reliability, diversity, computational efficiency, and resistance to collective errors. The framework is a research proposal; its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing methods require systematic empirical validation.

title: Development and multi-database validation of machine learning models for 28-day mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and pulmonary hypertension
abstract: Background Early mortality prediction in critically ill patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) coexisting pulmonary hypertension (PH) remains challenging, particularly because prediction models developed in intensive care unit (ICU) database may not perform consistently across other healthcare systems. Methods This retrospective multicenter study employed two large-scale databases to establish and validate ML models for predicting early mortality in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The MIMIC-IV database served as the model-development cohort (2555 patients), with external validation conducted on eICU CRD (292 patients) database. Six ML algorithms were adopted: Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The baseline variables were screened to identify potential predictors via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) regression. Model interpretability was evaluated via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Results The overall cohort consisted of 2,847 ICU patients with COPD and PH. Twelve consistently crucial clinical features were identified, including acute kidney injury, pneumonia, age, weight, heart rate, red blood cell distribution width (RDW), white blood cell (WBC), anion gap, chloride, creatinine, base excess, potential of hydrogen (pH). The Random Forest algorithm achieved the optimal performance, with a training Area Under Curve (AUC) of 0.938, internal validation AUC of 0.748, and eICU CRD external validation AUC of 0.800. SHAP analysis indicated that acute kidney injury was the most influential predictor, followed by base excess and RDW. Additionally, a web tool was developed in this study to facilitate the application of early death risk prediction in clinical practice. Conclusions This study is the multi-database validation of ML models for early mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The Random Forest model integrated with SHAP interpretability offers a reliable tool for clinical decision-making support, with consistent validity verified across two databases, including our internal validation cohort. This work provides a decision support tool to assist in identifying high-risk individuals within this complex comorbid population, and establishes a foundation for future studies with a more dynamic and personalized prognostic approach.

title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects

title: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE
abstract: We present Tulva, a practical threshold FHE scheme which equips a base FHE scheme with an asynchronous threshold decryption mechanism in a modular way. Our scheme simultaneously (1) is compatible with virtually any base FHE scheme and leaves its ciphertexts unchanged apart from an appended random tag, (2) supports a wide range of threshold profiles $(t,K)$ and ring degrees $\geq 256$ with 6-25 bits partial decryption per plaintext bit, and (3) achieves security in the presence of partial decryption queries on challenge ciphertexts based on the standard LWE assumption. We provide an open-source implementation, benchmark its threshold decryption performance and evaluate the end-to-end costs for typical privacy-preserving Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) use cases. For 16-out-of-512 threshold and a publicly preprocessed ciphertext, computing secret-dependent partial decryption and public share combination requires only 3.7 ms and 0.5 ms, respectively, on commodity hardware. Compared with the state-of-the-art synchronous scheme [Zyskind et al., CCS'25], we replace their ciphertext-independent yet interactive preparation of secret-correlated randomness with a public, ciphertext-dependent 0.5 s preprocessing step, eliminate interaction in the online phase while maintaining similar decryption time on the same machine, and support 32$\times$ more total users.

title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.

title: HankelKANet: Lightweight Path Loss Estimation via Physics-Inspired Hankel Convolution
abstract: Accurate path loss (PL) estimation is essential for wireless network planning and optimization. This paper proposes HankelKANet, a lightweight physics-inspired network for PL estimation that structurally embeds electromagnetic propagation characteristics into the neural architecture. Built on a single residual UNet backbone, the proposed model integrates urban layout features with a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network(KAN). Specifically, the convolutional kernels are parameterized by the radial amplitudes of the zeroth- and first-order Hankel functions. This formulation acts as a physics-inspired nonlinear distance encoding, enabling the network to capture dominant attenuation characteristics directly without requiring additional physics-based loss terms. Experimental results demonstrate that HankelKANet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on both the simulated RadioMapSeer dataset and the real-world Huawei RSRPSet. Compared with the leading baseline, PEFNet, it reduces the parameter count by 78% and lowers the RMSE by 16.96% on the simulated data, while further exhibiting robust cross-dataset transferability and high data efficiency during target-domain adaptation. To interpret these empirical gains, we mathematically establish a parameter-conditional spatial gradient bound. Using discrete Dirichlet energy (DDE) and Jacobian sensitivity heatmaps, we empirically verify that this physical encoding intrinsically constrains the network's spatial derivatives. This structural smoothness effectively eliminates non-physical spatial ripples, preventing overfitting to simulator artifacts and serving as the fundamental driver for robust real world generalization.

title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io

title: Federated Distillation: A Survey
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

title: Consumer trust in ai-generated advertisement content
abstract: Diplomsko delo obravnava področje sodobnega oglaševanja s poudarkom na vplivu generativne umetne inteligence na zaupanje potrošnikov. Problem izhaja iz hitrega napredka tehnologij UI, ki podjetjem omogočajo avtomatizirano ustvarjanje naprednih oglasnih besedil, slik in videoposnetkov, medtem ko se pri potrošnikih pojavljajo skepticizem in etični pomisleki. Delo temelji na teoretični opredelitvi koncepta zaupanja in k temu sodečih pojmov, empirično pa analiziramo odziv slovenskih potrošnikov na konkretni UI-generiran video oglas z uporabo prilagojene merske lestvice ADTRUST. V raziskavi ugotavljamo zadržano in nevtralno splošno zaupanje potrošnikov v UI-generirane oglasne vsebine. Potrošniki najvišje ocenjujejo čustvene, estetske in tehnične vidike oglasov, bistveno nižje pa resničnost in pripravljenost za sprejemanje nakupnih odločitev na njihovi podlagi. Nadaljnji rezultati potrjujejo, da splošni pozitiven odnos do UI vpliva na višjo stopnjo zaupanja v UI-oglase, medtem ko demografske značilnosti, kot so spol, starost in izobrazba, ne pokažejo statistično pomembnih razlik v stopnji zaupanja.

title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes
abstract: The training of neural networks often entails objective functions that are not globally L-smooth. For these functions, it is both theroetically and practically difficult to reply to the question: what is the largest possible step size that ensures the convergence of gradient descent (GD)? We address this longstanding open question in deep learning by providing a unifying definition of "large" step sizes that requires only local Lipschitz (or even Hölder) continuity of the gradient. We design first-order adaptive methods that provably yield large step sizes and show that they operate at the edge of stability (EoS) right from the start of the training. In particular, the loss decreases nonmonotonically and the product between the step size and sharpness, i.e., the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, stays above the EoS threshold of 2 throughout training. Using our method, we are also able to minimize the sharpness all the way down to its global minimum. Contrary to expectation, we find that encountering globally-flat regions too early in the training may both slow down convergence and jeopardize the generalization ability of the network. Exploiting a self-stabilization argument, we allow GD to enter slightly sharper valleys and turn unsuccessful training runs into very successful ones.

title: Antigravity HFS: Memory-Resident Debian Kernel & Loopback Hole-Buffer Guard against Trailing Viruses
abstract: Release Version 1.0.0 of the HFS (Hole-buffer File System) autonomous architecture. Combines a memory-resident Debian 12/Linux 6.12+ kernel (toram), kernel RAM disk (/dev/ram0), loopback sparse container (hfs.img on /dev/loop0), and cryptographic SHA-256 hole-buffer and sector slack space hashing to detect and neutralize trailing viruses.

title: The Great Enterprise LLM Decoupling: Weight-Space IP Contagion, Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility, Hardware-Enforced No-Learn Attestation, and Mandatory Third-Party Model Purge under Delaware Caremark Standards
abstract: Abstract: Global enterprise technology stacks—most notably Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) constituents and sovereign cloud operators—are executing an unprecedented structural purge of third-party frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), epitomized by the enterprise decoupling from external black-box providers ("Goodbye, Claude"). While superficially interpreted as cost optimization or routine vendor consolidation, this monograph proves that the decoupling is driven by an acute, existential legal and mathematical crisis: Weight-Space Intellectual Property (IP) Contagion and Fiduciary Liability Transmission. Building upon our forensic analysis of cross-border training data laundering (Project Panama, Record 23311531) and our Biological & Algorithmic IP Protection Covenants (NLL-v1.0-2026, Record 23358010), we establish four foundational results: (1) We formulate the Weight-Space Contagion Theorem, proving via non-diagonal Hessian cross-derivative coupling ($\nabla^2_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}$) that copyrighted works and sovereign trade secrets ingested during pre-training or fine-tuning cannot be surgically "unlearned" post-hoc without inducing catastrophic perplexity collapse (Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility); (2) We model Transitive Enterprise Contamination, demonstrating how API outputs, synthetic distillation, and IDE code completions transmit copyright taint ($\phi_{\text{taint}} \to 100\%$) directly into proprietary corporate repositories; (3) We design a Hardware-Enforced Zero-Gradient Attestation Architecture ($\pi_{\text{no-learn}}$) utilizing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$) to guarantee mathematically that enterprise inference and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) execute with strictly zero weight updates ($\nabla_{\theta} W \equiv \mathbf{0}$); and (4) We prove under Delaware General Corporation Law (Caremark standard) and SEC Rule 15c3-5 / Item 1.05 disclosure mandates that corporate boards retaining un-auditable third-party LLMs after receiving constructive notice of supply-chain IP laundering face personal, non-exculpated liability for bad-faith breach of the duty of loyalty. Finally, we codify a 4-stage Enterprise Decoupling Protocol transitioning global infrastructure from contaminated black-box APIs to sovereign, clean-room verified in-house AI stacks.

Building upon our forensic analysis of cross-border training data laundering (Project Panama, Record 23311531) and our Biological & Algorithmic IP Protection Covenants (NLL-v1.0-2026, Record 23358010), we establish four foundational results: (1) We formulate the Weight-Space Contagion Theorem, proving via non-diagonal Hessian cross-derivative coupling ($\nabla^2_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}$) that copyrighted works and sovereign trade secrets ingested during pre-training or fine-tuning cannot be surgically "unlearned" post-hoc without inducing catastrophic perplexity collapse (Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility); (2) We model Transitive Enterprise Contamination, demonstrating how API outputs, synthetic distillation, and IDE code completions transmit copyright taint ($\phi_{\text{taint}} \to 100\%$) directly into proprietary corporate repositories; (3) We design a Hardware-Enforced Zero-Gradient Attestation Architecture ($\pi_{\text{no-learn}}$) utilizing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$) to guarantee mathematically that enterprise inference and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) execute with strictly zero weight updates ($\nabla_{\theta} W \equiv \mathbf{0}$); and (4) We prove under Delaware General Corporation Law (Caremark standard) and SEC Rule 15c3-5 / Item 1.05 disclosure mandates that corporate boards retaining un-auditable third-party LLMs after receiving constructive notice of supply-chain IP laundering face personal, non-exculpated liability for bad-faith breach of the duty of loyalty. title: Matched-Capacity Comparison of Additive and Multiplicative Neural Network Surrogates for Response Prediction of Steel Roof Trusses
authors: Dr. V. K. Verma Deepak Kulyal
abstract: ABSTRACT Repeated finite element analyses account for most of the computational effort in designing steel roof trusses, and neural network surrogates can remove much of this burden. However, the influence of the neuron model on surrogate quality is seldom examined under controlled conditions. In this work, an additive multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a multiplicative neuron model (MNM) of nearly equal size (211 and 196 trainable parameters, respectively) are compared. Training data were drawn from a parametric STAAD.Pro database of 46,140 Fink, Howe, Pratt and Warren trusses checked against IS 800:2007, in which non-compliant designs were deliberately retained. Using nineteen input variables, each network estimated eight continuous responses together with a binary pass/fail design status. On held-out test data, the mean coefficient of determination of the MLP ranged from 0.942 to 0.946 across the four profiles, compared with 0.700 to 0.775 for the MNM. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors were 11–17 % and 26–37 %. Total weight was the most accurately estimated response (MLP R² ≥ 0.964), while the maximum utilisation ratio was the least accurate (R² ≈ 0.80–0.83), because the critical member shifts from one region of the design space to another. In pass/fail classification, the false negative rate of the MLP was 0.074–0.213, against 0.210–0.608 for the MNM. Since the MNM used a bounded geometric-mean aggregation and had marginally fewer parameters, its weaker performance is traced to the multiplicative form itself, which is poorly suited to the largely additive behaviour of truss responses. The MLP is therefore recommended as the surrogate, with its utilisation predictions regarded as the least reliable output. Key words: neural network surrogate, steel roof truss, multiplicative neuron model, multilayer perceptron, IS 800:2007, STAAD.Pro.

title: New PV output power forecasting approach using solar spectrum and deep learning for ultra-short time horizon
abstract: Accurate ultra-short-term forecasting of photovoltaic output is essential for improving the reliability and stability of solar energy systems. However, many existing forecasting methods rely primarily on irradiance-based features and do not fully exploit the information contained in the solar spectrum. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a two-stage approach to ultra-short-term forecasting of PV output current using solar spectral information. In the first stage, solar spectral irradiance is forecasted, while in the second stage, the PV array current is estimated to use the predicted spectra and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression model. The proposed method is compared with three alternative forecasting schemes. Firstly, a model based on statistical features of solar irradiance, including the moving-average clear-sky index (CSI ma ) and moving-average variance (σ ma ). Secondly, a model combining CSI ma , σ ma , irradiance, and spectral data. Thirdly, a model using irradiance, the white-to-total ratio ( wtr ), and sky images. Experiments were conducted using data collected in October 2025, and forecasting performance was evaluated for horizons of 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, and 60 minutes using R² score, MAE, MSE, and RMSE. The results show that forecasting accuracy decreases as the prediction horizon increases, with R² decreasing and error metrics increasing across all models. Nevertheless, the proposed spectral two-stage MLP-based approach achieves the best performance, with an R² of 0.971 for a 1-minute horizon and strong explanatory power (R² ≈ 0.87) for horizons up to 15 minutes. These results indicate that incorporating solar spectral information can significantly enhance the accuracy of ultra-short-term PV current forecasting.

title: Bayesian Learning to Select Fair Classifiers
abstract: Evaluations of classifiers (AI or human or agents) often assume a batch setting in which every agent produces labels on every example in a test set, which can be expensive or impractical in many contexts. This motivates online policies that adaptively select agents to query as examples arrive and update policies as outcomes are observed. We study the problem of selecting, in an online stream, the agent that best balances (i) predictive performance and (ii) subgroup fairness of a sensitive attribute, and that allows for delayed observations of true class labels. We formulate this as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit problem using Thompson Sampling, explicitly balancing accuracy and fairness. We conduct empirical evaluations on real-world datasets spanning problems involving tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, demonstrating substantial reductions in regret relative to baselines. Our theoretical contributions include guarantees on the performance of the selected agent that incorporate both the accuracy and fairness aspects of the problem.

title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
abstract: Exploiting temporal information in datasets with high temporal dependencies (such as spoken keyword recognition) by spiking models is still an open problem. Promising frameworks include Time-To-First coding (TTFS) and the inclusion of synaptic delays into learning. In TTFS, neurons are forced to spike at most once, forcing the network to found its learning on the spiking times of neurons rather than their spiking rate. Some models use the TTFS framework to directly compute the spiking time of Integrate-and-Fire (IF) or Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons. However, most models built in the TTFS framework have not been tested against datasets containing temporal information. Little is known about the latency of these models on temporal datasets, where the latency is the time taken by the network to correctly classify a sample. In this work, we study the behaviour of Delay Neural Networks (DeNN) models, i.e. models that directly compute the spiking time of neurons by bypassing the membrane potential and thresholding mechanisms of spiking neurons. We show how to analytically control their latency, and empirically study the latency-accuracy tradeoff in a dynamic temporal dataset.

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

title: Statistical Inference in Reinforcement Learning: A Selective Survey
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is concerned with how intelligence agents take actions in a given environment to maximize the cumulative reward they receive. In healthcare, applying RL algorithms could assist patients in improving their health status. In ride-sharing platforms, applying RL algorithms could increase drivers’ income and customer satisfaction. For large language models, applying RL algorithms could align their outputs with human preferences. Over the past decade, RL has been arguably one of the most vibrant research frontiers in machine learning. Nevertheless, statistics as a field, as opposed to computer science, has only recently begun to engage with RL both in depth and in breadth. This chapter presents a selective review of statistical inferential tools for RL, covering both hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction. Our goal is to highlight the value of statistical inference in RL for both the statistics and machine learning communities, and to promote the broader application of classical statistical inference tools in this vibrant area of research.

title: The use of artificial intelligence in the clothing industry
abstract: Diplomsko delo obravnava uporabo umetne inteligence v oblačilni industriji s poudarkom na personalizaciji uporabniške izkušnje. Predstavljene so rešitve, kot so priporočilni sistemi, predlogi velikosti, virtualno pomerjanje, personalizirano oglaševanje, napovedovanje trendov in upravljanje zalog. Rezultati anketne raziskave, v kateri je sodelovalo 140 oseb, so pokazali statistično značilno pozitivno povezanost med uporabo pripomočkov umetne inteligence in zaznano personalizacijo uporabniške izkušnje ter med zaznano personalizacijo in lojalnostjo potrošnikov. Ugotovljeno je bilo tudi, da imajo funkcije umetne inteligence pri nakupnem odločanju predvsem podporno, ne pa odločilne vloge. Učinkovitost umetne inteligence je tako odvisna predvsem od uporabnosti rešitev, kakovosti podatkov, transparentnosti njihove uporabe in zaupanja potrošnikov.

title: DecisionLens: A Canary Case Study of Request-Validator Misalignment and Fallback in Financial LLM Briefs
abstract: Structured generation and application validation can enforce different contracts, making an apparently well-formed financial brief unusable downstream. We examine this failure mode in DecisionLens, a system that combines deterministic financial evidence, structured generation, application validation, bounded corrective retry, and deterministic fallback. A completed Groq Canary crossed four synthetic, 24-month cases with five staged configurations (P0–P4), producing 20 final records from 22 journaled provider attempts. Eighteen attempts returned completed responses and four were recorded as transport failures; 19 finals contain reviewable content and one is unavailable. All four P4 finals used deterministic fallback. Offline replay shows that the three completed P4 responses satisfy the original provider-facing schema but are rejected by the frozen application validator. The request contract permitted free-text focus and action fields, whereas the validator required enumerated values and additional constraints. This establishes a specific integration defect in the tested configuration, not a general estimate of language-model factuality or safeguard efficacy. We document the failure paths, worked financial discrepancies, incomplete annotation provenance, and a subsequently approved but runtime-unverified contract correction. The study offers an auditable account of how schema compliance, application acceptance, output availability, and semantic quality can diverge. Four selected synthetic cases cannot establish comparative superiority, statistical power, or general hallucination reduction. This is an exploratory systems case study of four deliberately selected synthetic cases, not a powered confirmatory study, a peer-reviewed journal article, or evidence of general hallucination reduction. Semantic annotations remain incomplete; no finalized semantic performance rate or independent human-only evaluation is claimed. The held-out Main experiment has not been executed. Asadullah Hussaini is the sole author and takes responsibility for the research findings, interpretation, and final content. Partial annotations remain classified as AI-Assisted Author Adjudication, not independent human-only evaluation or finalized performance scores. Model-output quotations, quoted Groq Support wording, third-party works, dependencies and embedded font programs are excluded from the author's blanket grants; the supplement contains the complete license map and notices. Rights and reproducibility: GroqCloud hosted OpenAI openai/gpt-oss-120b. The three original returned P4 texts, model/provider attribution and content hashes are preserved. title: When Optimization Forgets the Minority: Bias Amplification in Policy-Gradient Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Bias amplification, the tendency of trained models to be more biased than the data that produced them, is well documented in supervised learning. We study it in policy-gradient reinforcement learning, where there is no static dataset: each episode belongs to a latent group that shapes the reward but is invisible to the policy. Under exact gradients the problem reduces to an averaged Markov decision process, so imbalance acts only through the weights of the averaged reward; the groups reappear in the variance of sampled gradients, and state visitation, which the policy controls, amplifies the effect of the weights. We separate the disparity induced by the problem from the disparity induced by the optimization. At the destination, with a full-support start distribution, unregularized softmax policy gradient drives to zero, at an explicit rate, the probability of every action that is suboptimal for the averaged problem; under strong imbalance these include the minority-preferred actions wherever the groups conflict. Entropy regularization restores a floor with closed-form thresholds in the bandit, where the regularized optimum is the ρ-average of the per-group optima. On the journey, near-deterministic policies are slow to leave (an action well), and in Markov decision processes the visitation distribution adds a second slowdown (a visitation well). In a gridworld where both groups share the same optimal policy, exact policy gradient from a fixed start state locks the minority out (its return stays 47% below optimal after 3·10⁴ iterations), sampled REINFORCE never finds the common optimum in 270 runs, and, with full state coverage, the time to recover the minority's goal grows faster than 1/(1 − ρ). Bias can thus be a property of the optimization path rather than of the data or of the optimum.

Bias can thus be a property of the optimization path rather than of the data or of the optimum.

title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

title: GLoD-LVSM: Learning Geometry-Grounded Continuous-LoD Scene Representations for Large View Synthesis Models
abstract: Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present GLoD-LVSM, a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, GLoD-LVSM learns a continuous field that initializes a flexible number of anchors to match the desired budget. A condenser then aggregates scene information into these anchors, with both the field and condenser trained end-to-end. Second, the condenser infers reference-token and anchor geometry to guide compression through geometry-grounded attention, improving rendering quality and enabling frustum culling during decoding. Compared with existing LVSM scene-compression baselines, GLoD-LVSM achieves the best trade-off between rendering quality and scene token count. Compared with the uncompressed base model, GLoD-LVSM reduces the scene-token count by 33.4% and accelerates rendering by $1.23\times$ with no quality loss. Under a relaxed quality-loss budget, the reduction increases to 85.5%, with $3.00\times$ rendering speedup. Further analysis reveals that view-synthesis supervision yields emergent scene depth and self-organized anchors that align with surfaces and adapt their density to local texture complexity. Beyond rendering, we further show that our scene representation also supports scene-semantic understanding, highlighting its potential for broader downstream tasks.

title: Loss-Tolerant Measurement-Device-Independent QKD over Untrusted Repeaters via High-Dimensional Time-Bin Multiplexing
abstract: We propose a loss-tolerant measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol using time-bin-multiplexed single photons entangled with local qubits stored in nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. In each round, Alice and Bob each send a single multiplexed photon to an untrusted intermediary, Charlie. Each photon first becomes entangled with Charlie's NV-center qubits; Charlie then performs entanglement swapping between his NV qubits to establish EPR pairs between Alice's and Bob's local qubits. With $d$ time bins per photon, $\log_2 d + 1$ EPR pairs can be generated per transmitted photon, substantially increasing the probability of EPR-pair creation under limited channel bandwidth. To further mitigate the effects of prolonged memory storage, the protocol employs a memory-insensitive (MI) architecture, where multiple banks of qubits and multiplexed photon routing reduce the effective memory lifetime requirements. This approach enhances loss tolerance, enabling higher secret key rates and secure key distribution over longer distances compared to conventional single-photon protocols. Using the Lo-Chau EPR-QKD framework and Shor-Preskill reduction, we prove that the protocol is secure without trusting intermediate nodes, making it suitable for quantum networks with untrusted repeaters.

title: Learning Graph Energies for Finite-Time Generation
abstract: Energy-based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is accurate at equilibrium need not yield accurate samples when the sampler stops after a fixed number of steps. We introduce finite-horizon energy learning, which adapts the acceptance energy of a Metropolis--Hastings sampler to the distribution it returns after a prescribed number of steps, with initialization, proposals, and annealing schedule held fixed. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals, and a learned energy governs acceptance. A training-only discriminator scores completed samples, and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of a proposal give an acceptance-gradient estimator that is unbiased for a fixed discriminator under stated conditions, without equilibrated negative samples or differentiation through discrete states. Generation uses the learned energy in the original single-trajectory sampler, without discriminator evaluations or reranking. On twelve pairwise binary targets with exactly evaluated terminal laws, learned energies have lower median terminal total variation than the equilibrium-correct energy in every tested short-horizon setting, and than its numerically tuned scalar multiple in most settings. On MOSES, a learned two-coefficient combination of pretrained Graph Energy Matching (GEM) potentials lowers FCD by 3.7--10.5\% relative to scale-calibrated GEM at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget and a sub-point validity trade-off at higher budgets.

title: Revisiting Triplet Contrastive Learning for 3D Shape Understanding
abstract: In multi-modal 3D pre-training, aligning 3D shapes, their 2D image counterparts, and language descriptions has made tremendous progress. However, we find that supervision from rendered images is unreliable, the semantics encoded in synthetic views are distorted due to domain gap, self-occlusion, and rendering artifacts. Instead, we learn transferable 3D representations from language only. We observe that, in real world, 3D shapes are organized in a tree-like structure, ranging from general concepts to fine-grained instances with specific attributes, while language typically denotes generic concepts and subsumes these various 3D instantiations. Hence, we propose to embed 3D representations in hyperbolic space, whose geometry is well-suited for modeling tree-like data without distortion. To capture the asymmetric hierarchy between language and 3D shapes, we further impose a partial-order relation that language entails 3D shapes. Our method, Hyperbolic Contrastive Learning (HyperCL), jointly optimizes a hyperbolic geodesic-based contrastive objective and an entailment loss to learn discriminative cross-modal representations while explicitly preserving this hierarchy. We also introduce a rigorously verified benchmark for comprehensively evaluating cross-modal 3D alignment. Across two widely used benchmarks and ours, we improve the performance up to 4.6% absolute percentage on 3D shape classification and 5.5% on cross-modal text-to-3D retrieval under the same parameter budget. The code and evaluation benchmark will be made publicly available.

title: Unified toolbox for multipartite entanglement certification
abstract: We present a unified framework for multipartite entanglement characterization based on the conditional gradient (CG) method, incorporating both fast heuristic detection and rigorous witness construction with numerical error control. Our method enables entanglement certification in quantum systems of up to ten qubits and applies to arbitrary entanglement structures. We demonstrate its power by closing the gap between entanglement and separability bounds in white noise robustness benchmarks for a class of bound entangled states. Furthermore, the framework extends to entanglement robustness under general quantum noise channels, providing accurate thresholds in cases beyond the reach of previous algorithmic methods. These results position CG methods as a powerful tool for practical and scalable entanglement analysis in realistic experimental settings.

title: Report on an AI "Code Camp" for developing a graphical sequencer environment for beamline automation
abstract: AI-assisted coding is gaining significant traction at the EuXFEL. Among all LLM use cases facilitated by the facility’s enterprise foundation model provider, coding related tasks have the highest token usage. In this contribution, we report on a condensed AI code camp. This intensive, hands-on exercise involved a small cross-functional team with diverse experience in AI-driven coding. The objective was to further develop a behavior tree-driven graphical sequencer for the facility, which is currently in a prototype stage. The task was to accomplish this within five days, taking advantage of agentic coding opportunities as much as possible. We did not succeed to develop an MVP but gained valuable insights into agentic coding instead.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement in Multi-Agent Systems: A Dynamic Framework for Individual and Collective Intelligence Optimization
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve their performance through individual learning and inter-agent cooperation. However, relying exclusively on individual reinforcement may limit the exploitation of complementary knowledge, whereas persistent mutual reinforcement may introduce communication overhead, correlated errors, excessive behavioral conformity, and dependence on potentially unreliable agents. These limitations motivate a dynamic framework in which agents adaptively switch between self-reinforcement and mutual reinforcement according to task conditions, learning progress, uncertainty, interaction quality, and resource constraints. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement (AS-SMR), a general framework for multi-agent systems. Self-reinforcement enables an agent to improve its policy through individual experience, self-evaluation, and locally available feedback. Mutual reinforcement enables agents to improve their policies through reciprocal feedback, cross-agent evaluation, experience exchange, and mutually informative learning signals. A context-sensitive controller estimates the relative utility of these mechanisms and selects individual reinforcement, mutual reinforcement, or a hybrid mode. The framework further incorporates reinforcement credibility, interaction costs, diversity preservation, and feedback-based switching to prevent unnecessary collaboration and unproductive isolation. The proposed framework is applicable to heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning systems and can potentially be adapted to language-model agents, robotic teams, distributed optimization systems, and other intelligent systems. We formulate the problem mathematically, describe an implementable algorithm, and establish research hypotheses and an experimental protocol for evaluating learning efficiency, collective performance, robustness, diversity, and communication costs. The framework is presented as a research proposal requiring empirical and, where applicable, theoretical validation rather than as an experimentally established superior method.

title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes
abstract: Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is challenging under unmeasured confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses unmeasured confounding through proxy variables, but existing proximal survival methods rely largely on restrictive parametric bridge models. We introduce Proximal Survival Bridge learning (PSB), a flexible doubly robust proximal framework for censored outcomes. Building on existing proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves, the framework yields outcome-bridge (OB), treatment-bridge (TB), and doubly robust (DR) estimators, with two flexible bridge learners: PSB-K, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and PSB-N, a neural estimator trained by a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. Unlike existing flexible proximal learners for scalar outcomes, PSB directly handles censoring and survival-curve targets. On a standard SEM benchmark, a proximal semi-synthetic ACTG study, and the real-world Framingham study, PSB-K performs strongest on SEM and ACTG, whereas PSB-N is the most stable on Framingham. Additional results with modern causal survival baselines, weakened or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring assess robustness across challenging settings.

title: Dual-Inertial Bregman Methods with Energy-Based Safeguarding
abstract: We develop a dual-inertial framework for convex optimization that introduces inertia in dual coordinates while retaining the Bregman proximal-type oracles. For unrestarted iterations, uniformly bounded positive directional variation gives a last-iterate $\cO((1+\log k)/k^2)$ rate, improving to $\cO(k^{-2})$ under additional weighted summability. A computable safeguarded algorithm gives a global $\cO(N^{-1})$ objective-gap bound for the best accepted point, where $N$ counts all proximal oracle calls. Under local strong-convexity and kernel regularity conditions, all three safeguarded methods restart finitely and attain a final-epoch last-iterate $\cO(N^{-2})$ rate. Numerical experiments compare objective accuracy and computational cost on entropy regression and nonnegative least squares. Comparative numerical experiments illustrate the performance advantages of the proposed methods.

title: Design and Analysis of Temporal Representations in Neural Networks
abstract: The ability to represent temporal information is often hypothesized to underlie the efficiency and learning capabilities of biological neural networks. This motivates the development of spiking neural networks. However, it remains unclear how temporal information is actually represented in neural networks and how different forms of temporal representation affect performance and computational efficiency. We introduce the notion of the degree of temporal representation of a neural network, defined by whether its constituent functions (activation, learning, encoding, and decoding) explicitly manipulate time as a computational variable. This perspective yields a continuum ranging from non-temporal representations, where time does not explicitly appear as a computational variable in the network functions, to fully temporal representations, where computations explicitly operate on temporal variables. Using a fixed deep architecture, we compare different encoding, activation mechanisms and decoding with increasing temporal expressiveness: non-temporal weighted-sum activations used in usual artificial neural networks, non-temporal binary spiking activations used in spiking neural networks, and spike-time-based activations used in delay neural networks. Experiments on event-based datasets show that increasing the degree of temporal representation improves both performance and computational efficiency, allowing state-of-the-art performances on the Google Speech Commands dataset. We further analyze how temporal representations induce distinct forward and backward computational trajectories, leading to gradients that depend explicitly on the history of event times.

title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

title: Bayesian local clustering of functional data via semi-Markovian random partitions
abstract: We introduce a Bayesian framework for indirect local clustering of functional data, leveraging B-spline basis expansions and a novel dependent random partition model. By exploiting the local support properties of B-splines, our approach allows partially coincident functional behaviors, achieved when shared basis coefficients span sufficiently contiguous regions. This is accomplished through a cutting-edge dependent random partition model that enforces semi-Markovian dependence across a sequence of partitions. By matching the degree of the B-spline basis with the semi-Markovian dependence structure, the proposed model serves as a highly flexible prior, enabling efficient modeling of localized features in functional data. Furthermore, we extend the utility of the dependent random partition model beyond functional data, demonstrating its applicability to a broad class of problems where sequences of dependent partitions are central, and standard Markovian assumptions prove overly restrictive. Empirical illustrations, including analyses of simulated data and tide level measurements from the Venice Lagoon, showcase the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed methodology.

title: PromptIQ: An AI-Assisted Prompt Analysis and Refinement System Using Chrome Extension, JavaScript and Rule-Based Scoring
abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are increasingly used for education, software development, data analysis, content creation and decision support. The quality and usefulness of their responses are strongly influenced by how users formulate prompts. However, many users do not have a systematic way to judge whether a prompt is clear, contextual, specific and efficient before submitting it. This paper presents PromptIQ, a browser-based prompt analysis and refinement system designed to provide immediate feedback while a user is interacting with supported AI platforms. The proposed system uses a Chrome extension to detect prompt text through a content script and pass it to a local JavaScript scoring engine. The current scoring model evaluates four dimensions: clarity, context, specificity and efficiency, combined into an overall score on a 0-100 scale. Functional testing of the implemented modules is used to evaluate the reliability of the system. The proposed system demonstrates how browser-based and rule-based technologies can be combined to develop an accessible, transparent prompt-quality feedback platform, with a future version expected to integrate an external language model for explanation and automatic prompt refinement. Keywords— Prompt Engineering, Large Language Models, Prompt Analysis, Prompt Optimization, Chrome Extension, Natural Language Processing, Generative AI.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Evaluation and Mutual Evaluation for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate the quality, correctness, relevance, completeness, and reliability of generated content. However, relying exclusively on self-evaluation may preserve a model's own biases and blind spots, whereas relying exclusively on mutual evaluation may introduce additional computational costs, evaluator disagreement, and correlated errors among models. This paper proposes an adaptive evaluation framework that dynamically switches between self-evaluation and mutual evaluation for multiple large language models. Rather than treating these evaluation modes as fixed alternatives, the proposed framework considers the selection of an evaluation mode to be a decision-making problem. Each model initially evaluates its own output, producing an evaluation score, an uncertainty estimate, and an explanation of potential weaknesses. An adaptive controller then determines whether the available evidence is sufficient or whether cross-model evaluation is required. The controller considers evaluation uncertainty, disagreement, historical evaluator reliability, task characteristics, and computational cost. Mutual evaluation is activated when additional independent perspectives are expected to provide useful information, while self-evaluation is retained when further cross-model assessment is unlikely to justify its cost. A feedback mechanism updates the controller using subsequent evaluation outcomes and, where available, external verification or human judgments. The framework is model-agnostic and can be implemented without requiring all participating models to share the same architecture or parameters. This paper presents the conceptual foundations, mathematical formulation, operational algorithm, evaluation protocol, and testable hypotheses of the proposed approach. It does not claim empirical superiority; controlled experiments are required to determine whether adaptive switching improves evaluation reliability and computational efficiency relative to fixed self-evaluation and fixed mutual evaluation.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Reflection and Mutual Reflection for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve their outputs through iterative reflection, self-critique, and collaboration with other models. However, self-reflection and mutual reflection have different strengths and limitations. Self-reflection enables a model to examine and revise its own outputs with relatively low coordination overhead, but repeated self-evaluation may preserve initial errors or reinforce an existing reasoning trajectory. Mutual reflection allows multiple models to identify weaknesses in one another's outputs and introduce alternative perspectives, but it may increase computational costs, generate redundant criticism, or encourage uncritical agreement. Existing approaches have investigated self-refinement, multi-agent debate, and collaborative reflection, but the choice between these reflection modes remains an important design problem. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Reflection Switching (ASMR-S), a framework that dynamically selects between self-reflection and mutual reflection for multiple LLMs. Instead of requiring a fixed reflection procedure, the proposed framework evaluates task difficulty, estimated uncertainty, reflection progress, disagreement among models, critique quality, and computational cost to determine which mode should be activated at each iteration. The framework also incorporates reflection-history tracking, evidence-aware critique, mode-switching control, and termination criteria to reduce unproductive reflection loops. A formal decision model, an operational algorithm, and an experimental evaluation protocol are presented. The central hypothesis is that adaptive switching can achieve a more favorable balance between answer quality, error detection, reasoning diversity, and computational efficiency than fixed self-reflection or fixed mutual reflection. The proposed method is a research framework whose effectiveness requires empirical validation rather than an established experimental result.

title: Integrating MATLAB-Generated C and C++ Fuzzy Inference into Embedded Development Workflows: Software and Supporting Materials
abstract: This software and supporting-materials collection accompanies the study "Integrating MATLAB-Generated C and C++ Fuzzy Inference into Embedded Development Workflows" by Goker Ariyak. It documents the integration of generated fuzzy-inference routines, FIS model files, and application adapters into established embedded development environments. The archive contains MATLAB generation scripts and example FIS files; the original 107-file generated C core; STM32F469 project sources; Arduino SAM3X8E/Digix sources using Arduino Due/SAM support; a Raspberry Pi C runtime; the author's separate Simulink/Waijung prey-predator model, FIS file, and MATLAB script; retained timing records and figures; independent source-comparison and rule-semantics checks; and archived ESP32 C++ sources with SPIFFS and FTP integration. The historical STM32F407 timing project's generated Waijung and legacy ST source files are omitted pending confirmation of their public redistribution permissions. The model inputs and associated evidence are retained. This limits the supplied reproduction materials for that example; no regenerated replacement timing build is claimed. Obtain any required vendor tools and libraries under their applicable licenses. The README describes dependencies, evidence provenance, and the scope of each component. The manifest records source locations and SHA-256 checksums. MATLAB Coder and Waijung results refer to distinct workloads and should be interpreted separately. The ESP32 material documents source integration; it does not supply a measured fuzzy-inference benchmark or a validated mobile-to-device deployment. Historical binaries are not included, and the ESP32 sketch contains credential placeholders. This deposit does not relicense the entire collection under a single open-source license.

title: Classification of quantum states through conserved operators
abstract: Determining whether quantum states can be interconverted by a prescribed set of transformations is a fundamental problem in quantum information. Here we develop a general classification framework based on conserved operators (COs), i.e., not necessarily hermitian matrices having the state of interest as an eigenstate. We first show that COs belonging to the algebra generating the allowed transformations can be obtained from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix. Their number determines the dimension of the accessible orbit, while their algebraic structure and eigenvalues provide further constraints on state convertibility. We establish general bounds on the number of COs and prove that highest-weight states, like separable states in the case of $n$ qudits, attain the maximum. We also show how these operators generate parent Hamiltonians having the characterized state as an exact ground state. We then also consider positive zero-eigenvalue COs, which encode forbidden directions of reduced density matrices and incorporate rank-based constraints into the same framework. Applying this approach to multiqubit SLOCC, we obtain complementary classifications from algebraic and rank COs. While for $n\leq 3$ qubits both lead to the usual classes, for $n=4$ qubits they distinguish 17 and 20 types separately, and 29 when combined. The combined classification yields 287 fixed types and $4$ continuous families for $n=5$ qubits, and 4926 fixed types and 147 continuous families for $n=6$ qubits, providing, to our knowledge, the most refined exhaustive classification of SLOCC-convertibility classes based on such data.

title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost
abstract: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.

title: High-Probability Regret Bounds for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling
abstract: Feel-good Thompson sampling (FGTS) augments the posterior of vanilla Thompson sampling with an exploration term that favors reward functions with high predicted optimal values. This modification achieves minimax-optimal regret up to logarithmic factors in linear contextual bandits, but existing analyses of its two standard variants establish regret guarantees in expectation. In this paper, we derive the first high-probability regret bounds for both cumulative and current-step FGTS in contextual bandits with general realizable function approximation. Our bounds depend on the corresponding decoupling coefficients and the prior mass near the true reward function. In the $d$-dimensional linear setting, both variants satisfy $\mathrm{Regret}(T)=O\big(d\sqrt T\log(2T)+\sqrt T\log(1/δ)\big)$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $T$ is the time horizon. This bound matches the dimension and horizon dependence of algorithms based on the upper confidence bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Relative to the expected-regret guarantees, the cost of controlling the regret with high probability is confined to additive terms with at most linear dependence on $\log(1/δ)$. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

title: A fast and frugal Gaussian boson sampling emulator
abstract: Classical algorithms have successfully reproduced expectation values of observables for certain quantum circuits using off-the-shelf computing resources; however, matching the performance of the most advanced quantum devices on sampling problems typically incurs extreme memory and computational costs, restricting such simulations to only a handful of supercomputers worldwide. In this work, we demonstrate a classical simulation outperforming Gaussian boson sampling experiments of 100 modes on established benchmark tests using a single central processing unit (CPU) or graphics processing unit (GPU). Being embarrassingly parallelizable, a small number of CPUs or GPUs allows us to match previous sampling rates that required more than 100 GPUs. We believe that algorithmic and implementation improvements have the potential to generalize our tools to photocounting and pseudo-photon number-resolving scenarios and larger system sizes. Last, most of the innovations in our tools remain valid for generic probability distributions over binary variables, rendering them potentially applicable to the simulation of qubit-based sampling problems and creating classical surrogates for classical-quantum algorithms.

title: A Web-Based Multi-Modal AI Framework for Intelligent Content Moderation with Constructive Feedback
abstract: Traditional content moderation systems primarily rely on punitive measures that focus on removing offending or inappropriate content without offering users any form of educational feedback or guidance. This lack of constructive interaction often leads to a poor user experience, leaving users frustrated and uninformed regarding the reasons behind content removal. Moreover, such a system fails to encourage long-term positive behavioural changes within online communities, as users do not gain insights on how to improve their conduct. This paper proposes a new constructive Artificial Intelligence (AI) intervention system that integrates a number of AI models in order to conceptualize content moderation as a limiting process rather than an educational process. The framework suggested in the paper combines HuggingFace's BERT-based toxicity analysis, SightEngine's image processing, and Google's Gemini large language model to provide end-to-end content moderation with construction of feedback. Based on comprehensive testing through user interaction analysis and comparative analysis, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of educational intervention in content moderation. The study advances the field by developing a novel approach to content moderation that puts user education and community development first while upholding safety regulations.

title: Explainable Prognostic Modelling for Glioma Using Interpretable Machine Learning Techniques
abstract: The problem of glioma prognosis, a fascinating one, is dealt with in the present study through the use of suitable machine learning and deep learning methods. These methods categorize the grades of glioma as LGG and GBM. The ensemble used is Random Forest, Decision trees, Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbor, Adaboost, SVM, CatBoost, LGBM, XGBoost, ANN, and CNN. Furthermore, an XAI was implemented to increase transparency and interpretability, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) being the primary evaluation. SHAP explains the importance of features and also explains prediction instances of models required for clinical decision-making. Advanced ML coupled with XAI improves classification transparency and thus builds trust in medical applications of AI. These findings encourage not only furthering the prognosis of glioma but also open up new possibilities for future research into medical AI applications.

title: A dynamic multimodal fusion model for evaluating interaction effectiveness in university English classrooms
abstract: Classroom interaction is a key focus in college English learning, but traditional assessments using delayed questionnaires or isolated behavior counts cannot reflect the rapid changes in the quality of participation. In this paper, we develop a dynamic multimodal fusion model that aligns speech, visual behavior, and the teaching environment within a 30-second time window, and outputs an interaction effect score that takes uncertainty into account. A prosodic-semantic speech encoder, a visual engagement encoder and a contextual event encoder are combined in a gated cross-modal attention module, and a temporal calibration layer adjusts predictions based on the lesson stage and class-specific baselines. Experiments used 72 recorded lessons from 18 classes and obtained 5,184 annotated windows and four interaction phases. Compared with late fusion, a temporal convolutional network and a multimodal transformer were used in the proposed model; it achieved an F1-score of 0.867, a mean absolute error of 0.214, and a calibration error of 0.031. Excluding contextually significant events decreased the F1 score by 4.9%, and adaptive temporal alignment reduced the mean absolute error by 15.1%. The model also found that interaction quality had dropped by an average of 2.5 minutes before observer-confirmed failures. evidence.title: A dynamic multimodal fusion model for evaluating interaction effectiveness in university English classrooms
evidence.abstract: Classroom interaction is a key focus in college English learning, but traditional assessments using delayed questionnaires or isolated behavior counts cannot reflect the rapid changes in the quality of participation. In this paper, we develop a dynamic multimodal fusion model that aligns speech, visual behavior, and the teaching environment within a 30-second time window, and outputs an interaction effect score that takes uncertainty into account. A prosodic-semantic speech encoder, a visual engagement encoder and a contextual event encoder are combined in a gated cross-modal attention module, and a temporal calibration layer adjusts predictions based on the lesson stage and class-specific baselines. Experiments used 72 recorded lessons from 18 classes and obtained 5,184 annotated windows and four interaction phases. Compared with late fusion, a temporal convolutional network and a multimodal transformer were used in the proposed model; it achieved an F1-score of 0.867, a mean absolute error of 0.214, and a calibration error of 0.031. Excluding contextually significant events decreased the F1 score by 4.9%, and adaptive temporal alignment reduced the mean absolute error by 15.1%. The model also found that interaction quality had dropped by an average of 2.5 minutes before observer-confirmed failures. Based on the above analysis, synchronous collection of multi-modal evidence and phase-aware calibration can achieve high-accuracy, interpretable results in real time for assessment and provide engineering support to augment teachers' professional judgment rather than replacing it.

title: AMARQ: Adaptive multi-application routing for quantum networks
abstract: Abstract Future quantum networks will have to support different applications on shared infrastructure, like fidelity-critical Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and latency-sensitive Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC). The existing approaches for entanglement routing either optimise for a single application, or rely on sequential resource allocation, which results in inefficient resource utilisation, unfairness and degraded performance when multiple applications compete for shared network resources. In this paper, we propose AMARQ, a multi-objective Deep Q-Network (DQN) based routing framework to jointly serve heterogeneous QKD and DQC traffic on shared quantum infrastructure. The agent makes adaptive and application-aware routing decisions to dynamically balance the rigid fidelity and latency requirements of QKD and the high-throughput and elastic rate requirements of DQC. The reward function combines a successful-routing throughput term with a per-edge fidelity penalty and an end-of-episode failure penalty; per-flow latency is enforced as a QoS constraint, and inter-application fairness is enforced by a dedicated admission-control loop that reserves a dynamic QKD qubit pool. We assess the performance of AMARQ on grid topologies with 25 to 625 nodes. AMARQ attains a request success ratio above 85\%, which is up to 32 percentage points higher than ESDI and 39 percentage points higher than Cicconetti, while keeping the end-to-end fidelity above 0.80 and the inference latency below 90~ms for all configurations.

title: A novel imbalanced learning using dynamic multiclass evolutionary oversampling sigmoid deep neural network techniques
abstract: The majority and minority class data variably reduce the quality of the data produced and make the network harder to train for class-imbalanced datasets. It is uncertain how the minority class data are distributed and how they are input into the model. Furthermore, due to their significant bias in favour of the majority class, typical machine learning classifiers suffer considerably. To address these issues, we proposed multi‑class data stream learning using evolutionary and oversampling (EVOS) techniques. Evolutionary feature selection and effective oversampling combine for multi-class data stream learning. The aforementioned procedures enable the generator model to produce realistic-looking samples of both the majority and minority classes by learning the beneficial characteristics of each. According to the experimental findings of the proposed approach, classification performance significantly enhances when compared to alternative state-of-the-art methods.
