title: Contrastive uncertainty learning for robust multi-structure segmentation in lower-pelvic MR
abstract: Boundary delineation of anatomical structures in prostate MRI is often compromised by regional ambiguity. Automated segmentation methods relying on global overlap loss functions tend to be insensitive to surface deviations, leading to significant errors in ambiguous regions. Most existing uncertainty-aware methods treat uncertainty as a post-hoc quality indicator or prediction filter. We propose Contrastive Uncertainty Learning (CUL), a supervised framework that uses predictive uncertainty to directly guide representation learning. Using Monte Carlo Dropout, CUL identifies voxel-wise uncertainty and structures the embedding geometry accordingly: low-uncertainty, correctly predicted features form stable voxels while high-uncertainty or misclassified features are actively repelled, preventing feature collapse at difficult boundaries. We evaluate CUL on a 589-scan 3D prostate MRI multi-structure segmentation task (8 anatomical structures) using a ViT with UperNet decoder architecture. Average Dice ($83.38\%$) remains comparable to the baseline ($83.35\%$), while surface distance decreases significantly ($p<0.001$) across 6 of 8 anatomical structures. A hard-case analysis reveals a $22{\times}$ asymmetry between significantly improved and degraded cases ($18.8\%$ vs $0.9\%$). Ablation studies show that removing uncertainty-guided sample selection eliminates improvements for the transition zone, while replacing the contrastive objective with a boundary loss additionally removes bladder improvements, demonstrating that both uncertainty-guided sampling and the contrastive objective are essential for the observed gains. These findings demonstrate that the proposed uncertainty-guided representation learning is a useful mechanism for reducing the risk of extreme errors in safety-critical medical segmentation

title: Bell inequality violation with vacuum--one-photon number superposition states
abstract: Entanglement is a central resource in quantum technologies, and the realization of photonic entanglement necessarily relies on interaction with matter. Resonance fluorescence (RF), originating from the coherent interaction between a driving field and a two-level system, plays a pivotal role in quantum optics. Here, we demonstrate a novel route to entanglement generation based on RF from a single quantum dot. Rather than relying on generation of multiphoton states, our approach directly exploits vacuum-one-photon number superposition states created under resonant excitation. By delocalizing this superposition via a beam splitter, we realize time-bin entanglement and observe a clear violation of the Clauser-Horn-Shimony-Holt Bell inequality using Franson-type interferometry. Our scheme removes the need for multiphoton generation, simplifies the experimental requirements, and establishes a scalable pathway toward solid-state entangled photon sources.

title: A PIPELINE FOR DEPLOYING AND MONITORING MACHINE LEARNING MODELS WITH DATA DRIFT CONTROL
abstract: A pipeline for putting machine learning models into operation is considered, com-bining automatic deployment, quality monitoring, and control of input data drift. A feedback scheme is proposed in which retraining is triggered by a drift index. Using an educational example, it is shown that drift control reduces the time to detect model degradation and the downtime on an outdated version without constant scheduled retraining.

title: From Biological Psychology to Artificial Psychology
abstract: Scretching Artificial Psychology (SAP): Bridging Biological Psychology, Artificial Intelligence, Neural Networks, and Digital Human Behavior This conceptual research paper introduces Scretching Artificial Psychology (SAP), a proposed interdisciplinary framework for examining the relationships between human psychological processes, artificial intelligence, neural networks, robotics, and machine behavior. Building on the functional similarities and fundamental differences between biological nervous systems and computational architectures, the study develops a task-conditional Neurodigital Correspondence Model (or Scretching Neurodigital Correspondence Model) and a six-dimensional Artificial Development Continuum to investigate artificial learning, adaptation, decision-making, behavioral complexity, and developmental capabilities. The framework integrates Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL), and the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix and Dynamic Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM/D-SDM) to examine human–AI interaction, perceived intelligence, trust, linguistic interpretation, and psychological attribution. Particular attention is given to distinguishing computational performance from biological cognition, subjective experience, and consciousness. Five proposed empirical studies establish testable hypotheses for evaluating neurodigital correspondences, artificial behavioral development, and human responses to increasingly sophisticated AI systems. The paper further considers the theoretical progression toward artificial general intelligence (AGI), artificial superintelligence (ASI), and possible artificial sentience without assuming that these capabilities have been demonstrated. Ultimately, SAP establishes a proposed research foundation for the systematic comparative study of biological and artificial intelligence while identifying new directions for cognitive science, digital psychology, robotics, AI evaluation, and human–machine interaction. Its models remain theoretical and require independent empirical validation. title: Endpoint law for temporal seriation: device data and code (EL v0.3.1)
abstract: Raw device data and code for a two-point test of the endpoint law for temporal seriation in quantum collision models (K. Tabuchi, EL v0.3.1, 2026). A system qubit interacts successively with three record qubits through fSim(0.9, phi) at phi = 1.0 (ideal alpha = 0.50) and phi = 2.2 (ideal alpha = 1.88) on Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q (Amazon Braket, 11 Oct 2026). The record contains per-circuit counts and metadata, pilot data, the qubit-set benchmark summary, task records, submission and analysis code, a 2000-replicate bootstrap re-analysis, a post hoc effective-channel fit and the pre-run noise-model simulations. Decision rules were specified before data acquisition but not publicly registered. See README.md.

title: From Models to Agents: A Closer Look into Agentic AI Systems
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence marks a shift from static prediction toward systems that perceive, reason, act, verify, and adapt through closed-loop interaction with external environments. Although large multimodal models provide the representational substrate for this shift, practical agency emerges only when model inference is embedded within memory, planning, tool use, environment interfaces, verification, and oversight mechanisms. We formalize the notion of an agentic AI system, distinguish it from single-turn assistants, scripted workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and classical embodied controllers, and propose a taxonomy covering model substrates, observation spaces, memory, planning, action interfaces, multi-agent coordination, evaluation, and autonomy constraints. We then synthesize learning and optimization paradigms for agents, including supervised trajectory tuning, tool-use adaptation, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, process rewards, verifier-guided search, test-time scaling, memory-driven adaptation, and distillation. Across domains such as web search, software engineering, multimodal reasoning, embodied control, scientific discovery, and enterprise automation, we analyze the factors shaping agent performance and reliability. We further examine benchmarks, evaluation protocols, safety considerations, governance challenges, and open research problems in long-horizon reasoning, memory management, multimodal grounding, and trustworthy deployment. A companion repository tracking developments in agentic AI is available at https://github.com/Tajamul21/awesome-agentic-ai.

title: Near-Linear Preprocessing for Range Weighted Longest Increasing Subsequence Queries
abstract: We give a deterministic data structure for range weighted longest increasing subsequence (LIS) queries on $n$ values with positive weights. Preprocessing takes $O(n\log^2 n)$ time and space. Value queries take $O(\log n)$ time, and an optimal subsequence of $k$ elements can be reported in $O(k + \log n)$ time. This resolves an open question on truly subquadratic preprocessing with polylogarithmic query time. The key is a single-crossing property of envelopes for value-separated endpoint sets, enabling $O(\log n)$-time persistent merges. The bounds assume constant-time exact addition and comparison of weights.

title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.

title: CktHGVAE: A Symmetric Design/State Heterogeneous Graph Variational Autoencoder for Transistor-level Analog/Mixed-signal Circuit Design and Analysis
abstract: We propose CktHGVAE, a heterogeneous graph variational autoencoder for transistor-level analog/mixedsignal CMOS circuits that takes not only design variables but also state variables as its inputs and outputs. With a single hyperparameter configuration without topology-specific tuning, comparison between model-generated and SPICE-simulated circuit operational states gives median R2 values above 0.9 for typical single-ended voltage amplifiers and the CMOS inverter, and 0.81-0.96 for differential amplifiers with larger datasets. Latent-space optimization in the PCA-reduced latent space with Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, random search, and quasi-exhaustive search is demonstrated for a common-source voltage amplifier with NMOS input and resistive load, where the objective function is defined as a penalty for deviation from required circuit specifications. For each search strategy, 93.3 - 100% of all design candidates suggested by the model satisfy the required circuit specifications at the decoder output, and SPICE simulations verify that 90 - 100% of them indeed satisfy the requirements. The model pretrained on a batch of topologies can be transferred to unseen topologies without retraining at all, with zero-shot reconstruction median R2 values of 0.72-0.90 in three of four scenarios, including transfer from single-ended to differential topologies, although the transfer fidelity depends on the choice of pretraining topologies. Our demonstrations suggest that the proposed model can potentially serve as a basis for AMS CMOS circuit design automation.

title: Differentially Private Learning of Markov Chains: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity for Item and User Level Privacy
abstract: Sequential data such as documents, conversations, and trajectories are naturally partitioned across users, motivating privacy guarantees that protect each user's entire trajectory. We initiate the study of privately estimating the transition matrix of a discrete ergodic Markov chain from N independent trajectories of length T, with arbitrary initial distributions, under maximum row-wise ell 1 error. Besides N, T, and the number of states, our bounds depend on the minimum stationary probability and the pseudo-spectral gap, which govern state coverage and mixing. Under item-level privacy, we give upper and lower bounds that separate the costs of sampling, state occupancy and mixing, and privacy. Under user-level privacy, we reduce the problem for sufficiently long trajectories to private product distribution estimation. Along the way, we establish optimal user-level private bounds for estimating products of discrete distributions, which may be of independent interest. In the user level setting, our bounds are nearly tight in the large T regime, whereas in the item-level setting, our bounds as tight up-to a non-private term.

title: Low-resource quantum energy gap estimation via randomization
abstract: Estimating the energy spectra of quantum many-body systems is a fundamental task in quantum physics, with applications ranging from chemistry to condensed matter. Algorithmic shadow spectroscopy is a recent method that leverages randomized measurements on time-evolved quantum states to extract spectral information. However, implementing accurate time evolution with low-depth circuits remains a key challenge for near-term quantum hardware. In this work, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical protocol that integrates Time Evolution via Probabilistic Angle Interpolation (TE-PAI) into the shadow spectroscopy framework. TE-PAI enables the simulation of time evolution using shallow stochastic circuits while preserving unbiased estimates through quasiprobability sampling. We construct the combined estimator and derive its theoretical properties. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our method accurately resolves energy gaps and exhibits enhanced robustness to gate noise compared to standard Trotter-based shadow spectroscopy. We further validate the protocol experimentally on up to 20 qubits using IBM quantum hardware. This makes TE-PAI shadow spectroscopy a promising tool for spectral analysis on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.

title: An Information Compass for Probabilistic Reasoning in the Brain
abstract: Probabilistic reasoning in the brain has been studied primarily using simple two-choice tasks that are experimentally and theoretically tractable but have unclear relevance to more complex problems. Here we generalize principles from these studies using information geometry, which treats probability distributions (``beliefs'') as points on statistical manifolds whose geometry captures relationships between those beliefs. We introduce an ``information compass,'' a context-dependent, one-dimensional axis along which an arbitrarily complex belief is reinforced or repudiated. Projecting high-dimensional belief updates onto this axis casts even complex decisions into familiar forms of deliberation and commitment used for simpler decisions. Our framework provides a unified account of how biological and artificial systems can use geometric forms of probabilistic reasoning to make decisions across a range of tasks and domains.

title: AI Context Association (AICA): Exploring Context-on-Demand for the Agentic Web
abstract: AI Context Association (AICA) is an exploratory technical concept that investigates how individual web content elements could reference external, machine-readable context that AI agents can retrieve when needed. Modern websites are designed primarily for human users, often presenting only a subset of the information available in underlying content management systems, product platforms, and enterprise knowledge sources. Embedding all potentially relevant information directly into HTML may increase page payload, while conventional APIs and integrations can require additional implementation effort. AICA explores a lightweight association between a specific web element and a separate context resource, such as a webpage, document, or knowledge source. The objective is to investigate whether this approach can help AI agents access richer, relevant information without unnecessarily expanding the human-facing page. The concept is intended to complement existing technologies rather than replace established approaches such as Schema.org, JSON-LD, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or WebMCP. Its potential value, interoperability, security implications, and performance benefits remain to be evaluated through implementation and comparative experimentation. AICA is presented as a research hypothesis and an invitation for technical review, not as an established web standard.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Mechanisms and Mutual Mechanisms in Multiple Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Intelligence Coordination
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance through internal processing mechanisms, including self-reflection, self-evaluation, self-correction, self-verification, self-planning, and self-refinement. Multiple LLMs can also interact through mutual evaluation, cross-model verification, collaborative planning, mutual correction, knowledge exchange, and multi-agent reasoning. However, neither persistent reliance on an individual model nor unconditional multi-model collaboration is necessarily optimal for every task. Individual processing may preserve efficiency but fail to escape persistent reasoning errors, whereas multi-model interaction may introduce communication overhead, correlated errors, redundant computation, and unproductive agreement. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Mechanisms and Mutual Mechanisms (ASSM-MM), a unified conceptual framework for dynamically selecting and combining individual-model and cross-model processing mechanisms. Rather than restricting the framework to one predefined pair, the proposed architecture treats self-mechanisms and mutual mechanisms as configurable action spaces that can be instantiated across reasoning, planning, diagnosis, verification, evaluation, learning, memory, reward estimation, and knowledge integration. A state-aware controller estimates task difficulty, uncertainty, historical performance, model disagreement, expected improvement, and computational cost to select an appropriate processing mechanism at each decision point. The framework supports remaining in an individual mode, activating cross-model interaction, returning to individual processing, or transitioning between different mechanism pairs. A cost-sensitive decision objective is introduced to balance answer quality, reliability, latency, and resource consumption. The paper presents a formal problem definition, an adaptive control algorithm, an implementation architecture, research hypotheses, and an experimental evaluation protocol. The proposed framework is a research design rather than an empirically validated system. Its potential contribution lies in the generalization of adaptive mechanism selection beyond a single task-specific collaboration protocol, subject to comparison with existing adaptive multi-agent methods and empirical validation.

title: An Interpretable Spatial Pathological Model for Subtype Prediction and Histomorphological Heterogeneity Analysis in Upper Gastrointestinal Cancers
abstract: Gastric adenocarcinoma (GAC) and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) are major upper gastrointestinal cancers with marked molecular, histological heterogeneity and poor prognosis. Even at the same stage, patients may show highly variable treatment response. Precise stratification can guide treatment decisions and prognosis assessment, but current molecular examination is time-consuming and costly for routine use. Currently, many pathological artificial intelligence (AI) models can predict subtype or response from whole-slide images (WSIs), but often lack spatial information and checkable biological explanation, which limits clinical translation. This study asks whether interpretable spatial pathological phenotypes can be extracted from routine pathology images to characterize histomorphologic and microenvironment differences across therapy-related strata and tumor-microenvironment niches. We will build a multimodal spatial pathological model that defines histomorphological phenotype clusters (HPCs), constructs a Spatial Pathological Topographic Map with Euclidean Rings (SPATER Map) at the invasive front of tumor, and predicts molecular subtypes separately for GAC and ESCC from images alone. We expect the model to link histomorphology with pathway activity and survival, These outputs may provide actionable histomorphologic and microenvironment evidence for precision treatment decisions and risk stratification, which may advance translation of spatial pathology models into clinical practice.

title: DefoliationCAM: An Edge-AI System for Real-Time Insect Defoliation Severity Assessment in Grapevines
abstract: Insect-induced defoliation threatens grapevine health and yield, yet severity assessment relies on subjective manual scouting. We developed DefoliationCAM (D-CAM), a solar-powered edge AI system that estimates canopy defoliation and transmits results via LoRa to a web dashboard. The pipeline uses YOLOX-Nano to localize grapevine cordons in 4K images and a MobileNet-based classifier with lightweight channel attention to classify 320 x 320 pixel patches. The 29,674 field-collected patches were labeled as background or one of four damage levels: no to negligible, mild, moderate, and severe. Merging moderate and severe classes reduced the class imbalance ratio from approximately 40:1 to 8.8:1. Synthetic augmentation increased macro-F1 from 0.768 to 0.838. The classifier outperformed ResNet-50 in macro-F1 with fewer parameters (1.08 M versus 23.52 M). Patch predictions were aggregated into a canopy-level Non-linear Global Defoliation Severity (NGDS) score and validated against an entomologist's ratings of 86 held-out canopy images. Quadratic discriminant analysis identified boundaries of 9% and 29% separating negligible damage, mild damage requiring monitoring, and action-level damage warranting on-site scouting and insecticide treatment consideration. The 29% boundary aligned with the 25%-30% action threshold range for Japanese beetle management in grapevine. Using TensorRT FP16 on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the pipeline processed each 4K image in approximately 1.5 s, with a complete operating cycle of 57-60 s. A five-week deployment of two field units demonstrated the feasibility of autonomous solar-powered operation, LoRa communication, and remote defoliation monitoring. D-CAM supports frequent, objective canopy damage assessment for targeted scouting and timely pest-management decisions.

title: OLiVES: An Outdoor Low-Light Video Benchmark for Enhancement and Segmentation
abstract: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). The dataset addresses key content gaps by incorporating a diverse range of natural textures, animals, occlusions, dynamic activities, and close-up scenes. To the best of our knowledge, OLiVES is the first outdoor low-light video dataset captured using professional cinema-grade cameras. It provides over 25,000 aligned normal- and low-light frame pairs, along with over 46,000 VOS annotations. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLVE and VOS methods on OLiVES and show that training on it improves performance on both tasks. The OLiVES project page is available at: https://anonymous-OLiVES.github.io/.

title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.

title: Instruction Mining From Images: Constructing a Synthetic Dataset for Multimodal Learning ILSP DCVLR Competition Submission
abstract: This work presents a compact and reproducible pipeline for synthesizing and curating image-based instruction-response pairs for DCVLR. We draw from the Cauldron collection and use Magpie-style instruction and response synthesis with Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct to create concise, image-conditioned instruction pairs. The pipeline consists of instruction synthesis, conditioned on input images and controlled via a system prompt, sanitization, tagging, and filtering of the instructions based on the score obtained by a reward model (DeBERTa-v3). We retain samples with positive scores to maximize the quality of the generated instructions. We observe that score distributions have a median and mean reward score of ~ 1.53 and ~ 1.75 respectively, indicating that most generated instructions are of good quality. The resulting dataset contains diverse instructions in the math, spatial, and social reasoning domains.

title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
abstract: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. A harness around the workflow's directed acyclic graph (DAG) decides which outputs may be used: it enforces mandatory checks, contains failures to the affected branch, recomputes from tracked versions, adds validators, and releases a result only if a risk model estimates its probability of being invalid as low. Language-model agents work inside the harness, choosing corrective actions and reviewing releases, but cannot override it. On 60 held-out paired instances of two workflows with injected faults, we switched components on and off. Each supplied a different property. Containment and recovery raised the number of correct results. Validation supplied safety: fixed rules without validation released 37 invalid results, while validating every candidate released none. Risk estimation supplied efficiency, matching that safety with 31% fewer validators at somewhat lower yield, although better targeting than random validation was not shown. Lineage evidence helped on one workflow. The language model added no measurable benefit: whether invalid results escaped depended on the harness, not the model. This proof of concept points to a practical path: placing agents inside explicit release-control structure can keep released scientific results trustworthy, and it gives more capable agents a measurable baseline to improve on.

title: Requirements for Teleportation in an Intercity Quantum Network
abstract: Abstract We investigate the hardware requirements for quantum teleportation in an intercity-scale network topology consisting of two metropolitan-scale networks connected via a long-distance backbone link. Specifically, we identify the minimal improvements required beyond the state-of-the-art to achieve an end-to-end expected teleportation fidelity of 2/3, which represents the classical limit. To this end, we formulate the hardware requirements computation as optimisation problems, where the hardware parameters representing the underlying device capabilities serve as decision variables. Assuming a simplified noise model, we derive closed-form analytical expressions for the teleportation fidelity and rate when the network is realised using heterogeneous quantum hardware, including a quantum repeater chain with a memory cut-off. Our derivations are based on events defined by the order statistics of link generation durations in both the metropolitan networks and the backbone, and the resulting expressions are verified against NetSquid simulations. The analytical expressions facilitate efficient exploration of the optimisation parameter space without resorting to computationally intensive simulations. We then apply this framework to a representative realisation in which the metropolitan nodes are based on trapped-ion processors and the backbone is composed of ensemble-based quantum memories. Our results suggest that teleportation across metropolitan distances already reaches the classical limit with state-of-the-art hardware when the data qubit is prepared after end-to-end entanglement has been established, whereas extending teleportation to intercity scales requires additional, though plausibly achievable, improvements in hardware performance.

title: How Loss and Maximum Error Relate to Taylor-Like Regression Coefficients When Approximating Cosine
abstract: A Taylor polynomial uses derivatives of the target function at a point, whereas polynomial regression uses training samples to fit across the entire interval. We ask whether having a better regression fit or a smaller domain lowers its largest error and brings its coefficients closer to Taylor coefficients. To test this, we compare polynomial regression trained using gradient descent (GD) to Taylor polynomials centered at zero for approximating the cosine function on intervals [0,4] and [0,10]. We vary training settings (viz., polynomial degree, learning rate, and number of training updates) and measure training loss (half of the mean squared error over 1,000 training samples), maximum absolute error, root mean squared error on [0,1], and absolute differences between the constant, linear, and quadratic polynomial regression coefficients and their corresponding Taylor coefficients. For degree 10 GD on [0,10] with learning rate 0.07, increasing the training budget from 5,000 to 50,000 updates more than halves the loss value but increases the maximum error by about 13%. After 50,000 updates using the same settings, the first three GD coefficients are closer to Taylor coefficients on [0,4] than on [0,10]. Further, increasing the degree from 18 to 30 using 10,000 updates and learning rate 0.07 reduces GD loss on [0,10] but slightly increases it on [0,4]. In a separate degree 10 least‑squares check, we find losses on both intervals are lower than GD’s using learning rate 0.07 and 50,000 updates. The constant, linear, and quadratic least‑squares coefficients are also closer to Taylor coefficients than GD coefficients from the degree 10 comparison described above. So overall, which method performs better depends on the chosen polynomial degree, interval, error measure, and training settings. Also, a lower loss can coincide with polynomial coefficients being closer to Taylor coefficients, but it does not guarantee such agreement. This upload contains the main paper and accompanying supporting material. Code is not included in this release.

title: Certified at the Source, Broken at the Boundary: An Effect-Based Threat Model for Random Number Generation
abstract: Random number generation is usually assured at the source: validate the entropy source, monitor its health, condition its output, and confirm the result passes the standard test batteries. That approach answers the questions it was built for, and deployed generators are better for it. But the historical record suggests it is incomplete. Most RNG failures didn’t produce obviously bad bits. They surfaced later, as shared primes, reused nonces, and recoverable keys, and they usually broke at a boundary between components. This paper presents an effect-based threat model for the whole generation chain: two security objectives, entropy and privacy; seven components from entropy source to consumer; four attack classes, covering state compromise, entropy reduction, availability, and substitution; and three positions, tagged by the layer where each weakness lives. It maps twenty-two documented incidents and demonstrations to the model and finds that deployed failures cluster at boundaries and in platform software, and that most were exploited passively, from public outputs. evidence.title: Certified at the Source, Broken at the Boundary: An Effect-Based Threat Model for Random Number Generation
evidence.abstract: Random number generation is usually assured at the source: validate the entropy source, monitor its health, condition its output, and confirm the result passes the standard test batteries. title: Ontology-Grounded RAG with SPARQL and Local Language Models for Technical Documentation
abstract: This paper presents LIDI-AI, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system whose knowledge base consists of technical documentation for the LIDI-AI Research Assistant, a web-based data analysis application developed at Universidad del Azuay. The runtime architecture integrates two complementary knowledge sources: an OWL 2 ontology (artifact version 2.0) with six classes and twenty-five properties (nine object and sixteen datatype properties) that models the five-stage pipeline, the accepted file formats, the statistical analysis types, and the system errors, and a SPARQL 1.1 query layer for structured intent resolution. A Prolog knowledge base built on an Object-Attribute-Value (OAV) representation, comprising 172 facts, 17 inference rules, and three diagnostic engines, is formally specified and validated as a symbolic reasoning layer, although it is not yet callable from the Python orchestrator at runtime. A lexical retrieval module selects ontology fragments as grounded context for a locally hosted language model, specifically Llama-3.2-3B deployed via the Ollama framework with Q4_K_M quantization. Evaluation on ten queries from real users shows that seven were resolved with high precision via SPARQL-grounded retrieval, two were resolved via lexical fallback with ontology traceability, and one out-of-domain query received an explicit knowledge-limit acknowledgment, yielding an appropriate response rate with zero hallucinations.

title: Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance
abstract: Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

title: Risk-calibrated knowledge editing for large language models in robotic decision support
abstract: In robotic decision-support systems, large language models are increasingly used as knowledge and reasoning modules to interpret observations, retrieve procedures, and support action planning. For robots operating in long-running and dynamic environments, reliable decisions depend on factual knowledge that may evolve through updated procedures, new observations, corrected records, and expert feedback. Such systems therefore require the underlying language model to absorb new knowledge over time without full retraining. Sequential model editing provides an efficient way to update specific model knowledge, but repeated edits can accumulate interference and degrade previously edited or unrelated knowledge. Moreover, existing methods often apply nearly identical update rules to all edits, despite the fact that different edits may have different levels of reliability and conflict risk. We propose RACE, a risk-calibrated sequential editing method that assigns edit-specific update and preservation budgets. RACE builds a compact risk profile from target support, paraphrase stability, and historical proximity, and uses this profile to formulate a constrained memory update objective. The objective writes new knowledge while anchoring conflict-prone historical memories, yielding a closed-form update for efficient sequential editing. Experiments on two standard model editing benchmarks and two large language models show that RACE preserves competitive edit success while improving long-horizon stability, which is important for maintaining reliable knowledge modules in robotic decision support.

title: CogDrift-4D: Hierarchical Multimodal Modeling of Temporal Behavioral Decay for MCI Detection
abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.

title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking
abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.

title: Quantum Folding in Chebyshev-Based Quantum Subspace Diagonalization
abstract: Quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) with a Krylov space spanned by Chebyshev polynomials of the Hamiltonian is a natural ground-state method for fault-tolerant quantum computers, but every guarantee it offers---convergence rate, noise floor, and the cost of turning its classical output back into a physical state---is controlled by the overlap of the reference state with the true ground state, which decays exponentially with system size for any product state and non-trivial Hamiltonian. We propose quantum folding: for a system governed by a local Hamiltonian, seed the QSD with the product of the ground states of its subsystems, which differs from the target only through the interface terms. We prove a nonasymptotic error bound for the Chebyshev QSD that is linear in the measurement noise, by transplanting Kirby's effective-Hamiltonian analysis to the Chebyshev--Krylov basis, and identify the block-encoding rescaling of the Hamiltonian as a parameter of the guarantee. Exact simulations of antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chains show that the folded reference state reduces the Krylov dimension for a given accuracy severalfold and lowers the error under noise by two to five orders of magnitude relative to the Néel state. We show how the Ritz vector is prepared as a physical state and that the ground-state generation probability obeys a tight ceiling set by the overlap, so that recursive folding prepares ground states at polynomial cost. Taken together, these results allow for a scalable QSD framework that avoids the exponentially small ground-state overlaps associated with conventional product-state initialization. Finally we compute the fold fidelity itself: a slow power law for the gapless spin-1/2 chain, a size-independent constant for the gapped spin-$1$ chain, and an exact closed form converging to 1/4 for the AKLT chain.

title: TVPara: Paralinguistic Captioning of Expressive TV-Series Speech in Complex Acoustic Environments
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) struggle to parse paralinguistics (e.g., emotion, pace, pitch) in speech that combines intense emotion with complex acoustic environments. Strengthening this ability calls for training data that reflects such conditions. However, existing corpora rely heavily on studio-recorded speech, offering limited emotional and acoustic diversity. To address this gap, we introduce TVPara, a paralinguistic captioning dataset built from TV series. Speech in TV series often carries diverse emotional expression and co-occurs with scene-specific background sound, providing expressive emotion and complex acoustic environments at scale. Constructed via LALM pre-annotation and human correction, TVPara includes two tasks: Single-Utterance (~492h) and Multi-Utterance (~213h) Paralinguistic Captioning. Fine-tuning open-source LALMs on TVPara yields an average relative improvement of 31.26% in paralinguistic understanding under complex acoustic environments. The gains further generalize to an unseen TV series and to cleaner, cross-domain speech.

title: SKG: A Law-Induced Engine from Inference to Induction
abstract: This paper proposes the SKG (Symplectic-Kernel Gradient) reasoning engine for law-induced inference and induction. Laws are a priori; data provide instances. Inference is geometric evolution under law constraints. We organize symplectic geometry, GENERIC, kernel methods, RKHS, group-equivariant networks, and constrained mechanics into a unified, analyzable, implementable, verifiable framework. We propose the SKG octuple S = (M, g, omega, H, S, G, Delta, Pi), whose four components correspond to four levels of laws: conservation laws, constitutive relations, symmetry groups, and axiom systems. Main results: (1) Invariants enter metric construction via the Jacobian: g = J^T Sigma^-1 J + epsilon_G I. For constant cases, we establish inverse reconstruction theory: solvability rank condition (Thm 3.9), consistency criterion (Thm 3.11), and uniqueness theorem (Thm 3.14). (2) The kernel bandwidth matrix is uniquely determined by Fisher information and satisfies task-independence (Thm 3.19). (3) The metric reconstruction error decomposes into four terms (Thm 3.21), with squared condition number kappa(Sigma^*)^2 as the dominant amplification factor (Thm 3.22). (4) For state-dependent cases, we establish function-space reconstruction theory on matrix-valued RKHS (Thms 4.8, 4.9). (5) Three-layer projections handle axiom, symplectic-step, and conservation constraints. (6) The residual equation yields the observable formula, four-dimensional rank condition, and noise propagation, while g_qq is structurally unidentifiable. (7) Kernel parameterization yields the RKHS extrapolation bound (Thm 4.15) and strict OOD gain theorem in group directions (Thm 8.15). (8) The learning-decoupling theorem (Thm 9.1) proves the sole object of induction is the parameters of the task energy. Validation: 1D damped oscillator and 2D rotation-invariant system; 6 unit tests, 10 experiments (paired t-test, p < 0.01).

title: Is there “Secret Sauce” in large language model development?
abstract: Abstract Do leading LLM developers possess a proprietary “secret sauce,” or is LLM performance driven by scaling up compute? Using training and benchmark data for 809 models released between 2022 and 2025, we estimate scaling-law regressions with release date and developer fixed effects. We find clear evidence of developer-specific efficiency advantages, but their importance depends on where models lie in the performance distribution. At the frontier, 80–90% of performance differences are explained by higher training compute, implying that scale—not proprietary technology—drives frontier advances. Away from the frontier, however, proprietary techniques and shared algorithmic progress substantially reduce the compute required to reach fixed capability thresholds. Some companies can systematically produce smaller models more efficiently. Strikingly, we also find substantial variation of model residual efficiency within companies; a firm can train two models with more than 40x compute efficiency difference. We also discuss the implications for AI leadership and capability diffusion.

title: FUQAROLAR MUROJAATLARINI SEMANTIK TAHLIL QILISH VA VAQT QATORLARI ASOSIDA MUROJAATLAR OQIMINI PROGNOZLASH MODELLARI VA ALGORITMLARI
abstract: Mazkur maqolada davlat organlari, xususan, ichki ishlar organlariga fuqarolardan kelib tushayotgan ko'p sonli va turli formatdagi murojaatlarni intellektual qayta ishlash, ularning mazmunini tabiiy tilni qayta ishlash (NLP) usullari yordamida semantik tahlil qilish hamda dinamik vaqt qatorlari modellari asosida murojaatlar oqimini prognozlash masalalari tadqiq qilingan. An'anaviy usulda murojaatlarni qo'lda ro'yxatga olish va subyektiv tasniflashdagi kechikishlar tahlil qilinib, matnlarni morfolojik va semantik vektorlash (TF-IDF, so'z embeddinglari hamda transformer arxitekturalari), mavzuli klasterlash, sentiment (hissiy kayfiyat) va shoshilinchlik darajasini aniqlovchi ko'p bosqichli matematik model ishlab chiqildi. Murojaatlar oqimining mavsumiy va tasodifiy tebranishlarini hisobga oluvchi SARIMA (Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) hamda chuqur rekurrent neyron tarmoqlar (LSTM — Long Short-Term Memory) integratsiyalashgan prognozlash algoritmi taklif etildi. Ishlab chiqilgan modellar va algoritmlar asosida «IIO-Analitika» axborot-tahliliy tizimining dasturiy prototipi yaratildi. Qashqadaryo viloyati ichki ishlar organlari misolida o'tkazilgan hisoblash eksperimentlari semantik tasniflash aniqligi F1-mezon bo'yicha 92.4% ga yetganligini, murojaatlar oqimini prognozlashda o'rtacha nisbiy xatolik (MAPE) 7.8% dan oshmaganligini hamda ijro intizomi va resurslarni taqsimlash samaradorligi 25–30% ga oshganligini ko'rsatdi.

An'anaviy usulda murojaatlarni qo'lda ro'yxatga olish va subyektiv tasniflashdagi kechikishlar tahlil qilinib, matnlarni morfolojik va semantik vektorlash (TF-IDF, so'z embeddinglari hamda transformer arxitekturalari), mavzuli klasterlash, sentiment (hissiy kayfiyat) va shoshilinchlik darajasini aniqlovchi ko'p bosqichli matematik model ishlab chiqildi. Murojaatlar oqimining mavsumiy va tasodifiy tebranishlarini hisobga oluvchi SARIMA (Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) hamda chuqur rekurrent neyron tarmoqlar (LSTM — Long Short-Term Memory) integratsiyalashgan prognozlash algoritmi taklif etildi. Ishlab chiqilgan modellar va algoritmlar asosida «IIO-Analitika» axborot-tahliliy tizimining dasturiy prototipi yaratildi. Qashqadaryo viloyati ichki ishlar organlari misolida o'tkazilgan hisoblash eksperimentlari semantik tasniflash aniqligi F1-mezon bo'yicha 92.4% ga yetganligini, murojaatlar oqimini prognozlashda o'rtacha nisbiy xatolik (MAPE) 7.8% dan oshmaganligini hamda ijro intizomi va resurslarni taqsimlash samaradorligi 25–30% ga oshganligini ko'rsatdi.

title: Confidential Narrative Intelligence on a Local AI Box: Epistemic Symmetry Theory with Algebraic Mixture-of-Experts Routing
abstract: Financial institutions want to read the narrative of markets with language models, but much of what matters most — internal research, positions, committee notes, client communications — cannot leave their perimeter. This report describes how Epistemic Symmetry Theory (EST), a framework that detects regime changes in market narratives and explains what changed, is designed to run entirely on a local AI box. The system is organized as a Mixture-of-Experts in which the experts are local language models assigned to distinct offces (measuring, embedding, answering, generating, verifying) and to distinct domain hyperspaces, and in which routing is decided by deterministic algebra rather than by a learned gating network: a small, fast recognizer chooses; a capable model answers; every composition of operations is checked before it runs. We describe the architecture, the confidentiality model — what stays on the box, what may leave and only by the user’s choice — the EST engine that runs on top of it, hardware sizing, and the limits of the current evidence. The report is conceptual: proprietary implementation details are not disclosed.

title: Stylometry or Embeddings? Authorship Attribution for Russian and Italian Poetry
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) embeddings achieve strong performance in authorship attribution, yet it remains unclear which aspects of literary style they encode. We address this question through a residualization analysis of two poetry corpora: 5,800 Russian poems (29 authors) and 10,400 Italian poems spanning seven centuries (52 authors). Using a progressive residualization waterfall, we subtract interpretable stylometric features and high-dimensional lexical controls from embedding representations to quantify their contribution to attribution accuracy. For Russian poetry, residual signal collapses to near chance (1.1×) after accounting for character n-grams and word bigrams, indicating that embeddings largely compress orthographic and lexical distributions already exploited in classical stylometry. For Italian poetry, a reduced but significant residual persists (4.6× chance), consistent with diachronic or dialectal variation not fully captured by standard features. We conclude that embeddings and stylometry rely on overlapping signals but differ in how they weight lexical, semantic, and historical variation.

title: Probabilistic Anchor Graph Projection for Tensorized Unified Label Learning
abstract: Although anchor-graph-based multi-view clustering has achieved significant success in handling datasets with arbitrary shapes, current methods still face several challenges. First, many anchor-graph-based methods fail to fully exploit the structural information of the anchor graph. They directly apply regression or decomposition to the anchor graph, overlooking the similarity information between anchor points and data points, which leads to suboptimal clustering results. Second, many anchor-graph-based algorithms only consider sample labels, neglecting the impact of anchor point labels on sample labels. A further difficulty is that an imbalanced anchor distribution may not represent the sample distribution faithfully and can propagate biased assignments to the sample labels. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Probabilistic Anchor Graph Projection for Tensorized Unified Label Learning (PAGP-TULL) method. Specifically, we introduce a label propagation strategy into the regression process of the anchor graph, obtaining probabilistic projections of both anchor point labels and sample labels. Additionally, we stack the soft label matrices of all views into a third-order tensor and impose a tensor Schatten p-norm regularization to fully exploit the high-order complementary information and spatial low-rank structures embedded across different views. Furthermore, we introduce concept regression to reduce the number of variables and thus lower the algorithm’s complexity. We also fully exploit the structural information of the anchor graph, using anchor point labels to guide the learning of sample labels. At the same time, we design a novel balanced regularization term to prevent the occurrence of two trivial solutions for anchor point labels, thereby improving the robustness and performance of the method. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and superiority of the PAGP-TULL method.

title: Structural control of two-level defect density revealed by high-throughput correlative measurements of Josephson junctions
abstract: Materials defects in Josephson junctions (JJs), often referred to as two-level systems (TLS), couple to superconducting qubits and are a critical bottleneck for scalable quantum processors. Despite their importance, understanding the microscopic sources of TLS and how to mitigate them has remained a major challenge. Here, we demonstrate a high-throughput, correlated approach to trace the microstructural origins of strongly-coupled TLS in Josephson circuits. We assembled a massive dataset of TLS across 6000 Al/AlOx/Al JJs and more than 600 atomic resolution transmission electron microscopy images. We statistically link fabrication, microstructure, and TLS occurrence, revealing a strong correlation between Al electrode thickness, Al grain size, and TLS density. Correspondingly, we find a two-thirds reduction in TLS prompted by a change in electrode fabrication parameters. These results demonstrate a robust, data-driven methodology to understand and control defects in quantum circuits and pave the way for significantly reducing TLS density.

title: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multi-Stream Quickest Change Detection
abstract: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework is proposed for quickest change detection (QCD) where there are multiple experts, and each expert produces a sequence of statistics for change detection. A change is declared when a weighted sum of these statistics crosses a threshold. This framework is then applied to the problem of multi-stream QCD to obtain a family of powerful algorithms that outperform the best known algorithms in the literature. In the multi-stream QCD problem, a decision-maker observes multiple streams of observations. At the change point, the distribution of an unknown subset of the streams changes. The optimal algorithm based on a generalized likelihood ratio is computationally expensive. One of the most computationally and performance-efficient algorithms in the literature is the rank-weighted sum (RWS) scheme based on Shiryaev-Roberts statistics. It is shown in the paper that the MoE-based QCD algorithm for multi-stream data outperforms the RWS scheme. This is demonstrated through simulation results on real-valued Gaussian mean shift data and high-dimensional data from Gaussian--Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machines (GB-RBMs).

title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition
abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.

title: Revisiting Non-Adaptive Set Membership Schemes: Removing the Logarithmic Factor
abstract: We study non-adaptive bit-probe schemes for static set membership. Each query reads a fixed number of bits and answers by strict majority. We revisit the random bipartite-graph construction of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017]. The main observation is that a slightly stronger expansion property already bounds the number of exceptional elements. This makes a separate probabilistic estimate for exceptional elements unnecessary. A detailed union-bound calculation then gives, for every fixed $t\ge5$, a logarithm-free existence bound of $O_t(m^{1/c}n^{1-1/c})$, where $c=\lfloor(t-1)/2\rfloor$. For odd $t$, this removes the logarithmic factor from the general upper bound of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017].

title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence
abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.

title: KORXONALAR FAOLIYATIDA MIJOZLARGA XIZMAT KO‘RSATISHDA SUN’IY INTELLEKT (CHAT-BOTLAR)NING IQTISODIY SAMARADORLIGI
abstract: Ushbu maqolada raqamli iqtisodiyot sharoitida O‘zbekistondagi kichik va o‘rta biznes subyektlari faoliyatida sun’iy intellekt texnologiyalarining, xususan, aqlli muloqot botlarining (chat-botlar) mijozlarga xizmat ko‘rsatishdagi iqtisodiy afzalliklari tahlil qilingan. Tadqiqotning asosiy maqsadi – kichik va o‘rta biznes korxonalarida an’anaviy inson mehnatiga asoslangan aloqa xizmatlaridan voz kechib, sun’iy intellekt botlarini joriy etishning moliyaviy rentabelligini miqdoriy jihatdan baholashdan iborat. Mavzuning dolzarbligi shundaki, an’anaviy aloqa markazlari (operatorlar faoliyati) hamda raqamli muloqot dasturlarining doimiy va o‘zgaruvchan xarajatlari o‘rtasidagi farq korxonalarda moliyaviy tejamkorlikni ta’minlashda hal qiluvchi ahamiyat kasb etmoqda. Tadqiqot metodologiyasi doirasida iqtisodiy-matematik modellashtirish, qiyosiy tahlil va kuzatuv usullaridan foydalanildi. Olingan asosiy natijalar shuni ko‘rsatadiki, raqamli usulga o‘tish korxonaning xizmat ko‘rsatish bilan bog‘liq xarajatlarini salkam 85 foizga qisqartiradi hamda xaridorlarning 70 foizi aynan algoritmik muloqotni afzal ko‘radi. Taklif etilayotgan yondashuvning ilmiy yangiligi shundan iboratki, sun’iy intellektning bevosita mikrodarajadagi (bitta mijozga xizmat ko‘rsatish tannarxi) iqtisodiy samaradorligi raqamlarda ifodalangan. Uning amaliy ahamiyati esa xizmat ko‘rsatish sohasiga aqlli texnologiyalarni integratsiya qilish bo‘yicha aniq xulosa va tavsiyalar ishlab chiqilganligida namoyon bo‘ladi.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Verification and Mutual Verification in Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate plausible but incorrect responses, and their ability to verify their own outputs is limited by uncertainty, shared reasoning biases, and insufficient access to independent evidence. Self-verification allows a model to inspect its own output, whereas mutual verification enables multiple models to evaluate one another's responses. However, relying exclusively on either mode may be inefficient or unreliable: self-verification can preserve the original model's errors, while mutual verification introduces additional computational costs and may propagate correlated mistakes. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Verification (ASMV), a framework that dynamically switches between self-verification and mutual verification according to the estimated verification requirements of each generated response. The framework consists of an initial generation stage, a self-verification stage, a verification-state estimator, an adaptive mode-selection controller, a mutual-verification stage, and a final decision module. The controller considers uncertainty, disagreement, estimated error severity, verification history, evidence availability, and computational cost to determine whether a model should continue checking its own output or request verification from other models. Rather than treating self-verification and mutual verification as mutually exclusive system designs, ASMV treats them as complementary operational modes within a unified decision process. The paper formulates the framework mathematically, specifies an implementable algorithm, develops testable research hypotheses, and proposes an evaluation protocol covering reasoning accuracy, factuality, calibration, verification efficiency, and robustness. Because the framework has not yet been empirically evaluated in this paper, its expected benefits are presented as hypotheses rather than established results. The proposed research aims to investigate whether adaptive verification can provide a more effective balance between reliability, computational expenditure, and resistance to shared model errors than fixed verification strategies.

title: Requested Budgets, Realized Reasoning, and Answer Accuracy: An Empirical Audit of L1-Exact on MATH-500
abstract: Prompted token budgets provide a practical interface for allocating reasoning compute, but interpreting their effects requires specifying both the token boundary and the answer-scoring policy. We audit a pinned release of L1-Qwen-1.5B-Exact on all 500 MATH-500 problems at four requested budgets, with 16 seeded generations per problem and budget: 32,000 generations in total. Mean delimited reasoning lengths are 356, 865, 1,773, and 3,259 tokens for requests of 512, 1,024, 2,048, and 3,600; corresponding mean complete-output lengths are 400, 1,038, 2,040, and 3,537. The distinction is consistent with L1's complete-output training objective, and materially changes the measured adherence to the requested budget. Under the accepted evaluation workflow, answer accuracy is 69.16%, 77.04%, 80.24%, and 83.03%. The gain from the smallest to largest request is 13.86 percentage points, with a paired problem-bootstrap 95% interval of [11.60, 16.11]. The grading provenance is explicit: 31,567 deterministic comparisons, 405 AI judgments, and 28 single-reviewer human judgments. Twenty-seven accepted answers occur in unfinished reasoning outputs; requiring a closed reasoning boundary changes accuracy at the largest budget to 82.79%. We report this sensitivity, problem-difficulty heterogeneity, and immutable artifacts. Complete-output central 90% length intervals are disjoint across adjacent budgets, despite tail overlap in the observed ranges. The study is a checkpoint-specific measurement and replication audit, rather than a causal law of realized reasoning length or an independently human-validated accuracy benchmark. evidence.title: Requested Budgets, Realized Reasoning, and Answer Accuracy: An Empirical Audit of L1-Exact on MATH-500
evidence.abstract: Prompted token budgets provide a practical interface for allocating reasoning compute, but interpreting their effects requires specifying both the token boundary and the answer-scoring policy. We audit a pinned release of L1-Qwen-1.5B-Exact on all 500 MATH-500 problems at four requested budgets, with 16 seeded generations per problem and budget: 32,000 generations in total. Mean delimited reasoning lengths are 356, 865, 1,773, and 3,259 tokens for requests of 512, 1,024, 2,048, and 3,600; corresponding mean complete-output lengths are 400, 1,038, 2,040, and 3,537. The distinction is consistent with L1's complete-output training objective, and materially changes the measured adherence to the requested budget. Under the accepted evaluation workflow, answer accuracy is 69.16%, 77.04%, 80.24%, and 83.03%. The gain from the smallest to largest request is 13.86 percentage points, with a paired problem-bootstrap 95% interval of [11.60, 16.11]. The grading provenance is explicit: 31,567 deterministic comparisons, 405 AI judgments, and 28 single-reviewer human judgments. Twenty-seven accepted answers occur in unfinished reasoning outputs; requiring a closed reasoning boundary changes accuracy at the largest budget to 82.79%. We report this sensitivity, problem-difficulty heterogeneity, and immutable artifacts. Complete-output central 90% length intervals are disjoint across adjacent budgets, despite tail overlap in the observed ranges. The study is a checkpoint-specific measurement and replication audit, rather than a causal law of realized reasoning length or an independently human-validated accuracy benchmark. title: A Cascaded-XCViT based Few-shot Classification Algorithm for Breast Ultrasound Images
abstract: Breast ultrasound serves as a cornerstone non-invasive technique for the screening and diagnosis of breast diseases. To address the challenge of limited feature generalization in few-shot learning for breast ultrasound image classification, this study proposes a novel cascaded Cross-Covariance Vision Transformer (XCViT) framework. A dual-stage architecture is introduced. Stage A employs hierarchical feature distillation via a three-level cascaded-XCViT module with Teacher–Student frameworks, generating dual-path tokens and utilizing token spectral clustering for semantic downsampling. Stage B uses frozen encoder outputs to derive prototype vectors from support-set features, enabling training-free inference via distance metric learning. Evaluation showed accuracies of 79.8% (1-shot) and 89.7% (5-shot) on CIFAR-FS, 47.2% (1-shot) and 67.3% (5-shot) on FC100, and 61.5% (5-shot) on a clinical breast ultrasound dataset, outperforming existing methods by 2.0–5.6%. The method demonstrates strong performance in low-data regimes and offers a promising solution for few-shot clinical auxiliary diagnosis.

title: Machine-learning-based neutrino-event generation constrained by experimental measurements
abstract: We present a generative surrogate for charged-current \(ν_μ\)-nucleus scattering that can be calibrated to measured differential cross sections without event-level experimental samples. Starting from a theoretical interaction model, we fine-tune the surrogate to a MicroBooNE measurement and show that this also improves the description of observables not used in the fit. The calibrated model can also be applied to measurements from different neutrino fluxes without retuning, while retaining event-level predictions of outgoing-muon kinematics. Our results show that experimental cross sections can directly constrain generative event models while preserving their applicability across different observables and beam configurations.

title: Convergence Rates of Gaussian Process Thompson Sampling for Efficient Global Optimization
abstract: Efficient global optimization aims to identify a global optimum of an expensive black-box function within a limited evaluation budget $N$. We investigate the convergence rates of Gaussian process Thompson sampling (GP-TS) under noiseless observations, assuming a fixed objective function in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). For Matérn kernels with smoothness parameter $ν$ in dimension $d$, we establish a worst-case expected simple-regret upper bound of $O(N^{-ν/d}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both discrete GP-TS on sufficiently fine grids and its continuous counterpart. For the continuous implementation, we develop a nested-grid argument to control posterior sample paths over the entire domain. We further establish matching lower bounds of $Ω(N^{-5/2}\sqrt{\log N})$ for both implementations under a fixed one-dimensional Matérn-$5/2$ kernel, demonstrating that the logarithmic penalty is intrinsic to standard GP-TS in this setting. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Gaussian Process Capped Thompson Sampling (GP-CTS), which caps posterior sample paths using a valid RKHS norm upper bound while preserving optimism. This modification successfully eliminates the logarithmic penalty and achieves the minimax-optimal rate $Θ(N^{-ν/d})$ for both discrete and continuous implementations.

title: Collective kernel EFT for pre-activation ResNets
abstract: Abstract In finite-width deep neural networks, the empirical kernel G evolves stochastically across layers. We develop a collective kernel effective field theory (EFT) for a simplified pre-activation residual model. Exact conditional Gaussianity of the residual increment gives finite-width discrete identities for G and its sigma-kernel source. A projected G-only closure and a continuous-depth approximation define reference equations for the mean kernel K0, the kernel covariance V4, and the next-to-leading mean correction K1. Numerical tests show that this closure captures the leading mean-kernel evolution, whereas its covariance and next-to-leading accuracy depend on sigma-kernel modes omitted from the G-only state. For the scalar (N=1) model with tanh activation, a Hermite--Galerkin extension agrees with the extrapolated K1 value and reduces the V4 endpoint error by 85-93% relative to the G-only reference. These results clarify the range of validity of the equal-time Markov G-only description and identify the additional collective information required beyond it.

title: From complete channel order to capacity and one-way distillation
abstract: A universal construction that converts failure of complete quantum-channel information order into strictly positive ordinary private and quantum capacity. It claims an exact-zero capacity undecidability classification for finite rational-complex memoryless channels and corresponding positivity and zero classifications for one-way distillable entanglement and secret key. The state reductions retain any prescribed two-way distillation lower bound. The construction explicitly charges reference transmission and activation helper uses to the constructed channel. Strict positivity is distinguished from any uniform positive capacity gap; fixed-error capacity inapproximability is not claimed. The exact order-equivalence and undecidability premises are developed in the companion manuscript Complete information orders of quantum channels: equivalence and undecidability.

title: Text-to-Speech Bahasa Melayu Dialek Lubuk Kandis Menggunakan Metode VITS
abstract: The existence of numerous regional languages in Indonesia reflects the country's cultural richness, with their historical distribution forming various dialects. One of them is the Malay Language of the Lubuk Kandis Dialect. To support the preservation and dissemination of this language, this study applies speech synthesis technology in the form of Text-to-Speech (TTS) to generate speech output for the Lubuk Kandis dialect. A dataset consisting of 500 daily activity sentences was recorded by a native speaker of Lubuk Kandis and validated by a local linguistic expert. The Variational Inference with Adversarial Learning for End-to-End Text-to-Speech (VITS) method was adopted to produce speech output that resembles natural human voice. The evaluation used the Mean Opinion Score (MOS) test involving five respondents and resulted in an average score of 4.72, indicating that the generated speech falls into the good category. These findings demonstrate that the VITS method is effective in synthesizing natural and intelligible speech for the Malay Language of the Lubuk Kandis Dialect, providing potential support for the preservation of regional languages.

title: A Lightweight Lattice-Based Post-Quantum Cryptographic Protocol for Secure Key Establishment in Resource-Constrained IoT Edge Devices
abstract: In this work, a lightweight post-quantum cryptographic protocol specifically designed for resource-constrained IoT edge devices is presented, addressing the vulnerability of conventional encryption to quantum computing attacks. The proposed protocol employs a modified NTRU-based algorithm with reduced parameter sizes, achieving switch production in 12.4 ms, encryption in 8.2 ms, and total energy consumption of 4.2 mJ per exchange - 63% lower than standard post-quantum protocols. Experimental results demonstrate resistance against quantum attacks exceeding 1018 processes while maintaining response times under 50 ms, with a compression mechanism reducing message size to 186 bytes. The protocol achieves an optimal balance between post-quantum security and operational efficiency, offering a practical solution for narrow-bandwidth, battery-limited IoT environments.
